title: Quiz 2 Review - Processes, Threads, IPC, Race Conditions, Semaphores, Mutexes
notes: A process is an abstraction of a running program, including the program counter, registers, and variables needed to resume execution.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Multiprogramming rapidly switches the CPU among processes, creating pseudoparallelism even though only one process runs at an instant.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Each process conceptually has its own virtual CPU, but the physical CPU loads and saves each process’s program counter during switches.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Processes must not assume fixed timing because CPU scheduling and interrupts can change how long a process runs before being preempted.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
A program is passive code stored on disk, while a process is an active execution with state, input, output, and progress.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Running the same program twice counts as two separate processes, even if the operating system shares the read-only program text in memory.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Processes can be created during system initialization, by process-creation system calls, by user requests, or by initiating batch jobs.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
In UNIX, fork creates a child that is a clone of the parent, and execve is typically used afterward to run a different program.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
UNIX uses fork then execve so the child can adjust file descriptors for redirection before replacing its memory image.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
In Windows, CreateProcess creates a new process and loads the target program in one call with many configuration parameters.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Processes terminate by normal exit, voluntary error exit, fatal error, or being killed by another authorized process.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
UNIX can form process hierarchies where init is the root of a system-wide process tree created at boot time.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Windows does not enforce a permanent process hierarchy, and process handles can be passed to other processes.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
A process can be running, ready, or blocked; blocked means it cannot run even if the CPU is idle.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Transitions between running and ready are controlled by the scheduler, while blocked to ready occurs when the awaited event happens.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
The OS maintains a process table with one entry per process, storing state like program counter, stack pointer, and open file status.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Interrupt hardware saves key state and jumps via the interrupt vector, and software then saves registers and invokes scheduling logic.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Interrupt handling often begins in assembly because saving registers and switching stacks cannot be expressed reliably in high-level languages.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
CPU utilization under multiprogramming can be modeled as 1 − p^n where p is I/O-wait fraction and n is degree of multiprogramming.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
In traditional systems, a process has one address space and one thread of control, but multithreading allows multiple control flows per process.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Threads are useful because multiple activities can block independently while still sharing the same address space and data.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Threads are lighter weight than processes and can be created 10–100 times faster in many systems, enabling dynamic concurrency.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Threads improve performance when computation overlaps with I/O, but provide no speedup if all threads are purely CPU bound.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
In the classical thread model, processes group resources like address space and files, while threads are scheduled entities with PC and stack.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Threads in the same process share global variables and can even corrupt each other’s stacks, so correctness requires cooperation and synchronization.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Interprocess communication requires both communication and coordination because shared resources can cause conflicts and dependencies.

A race condition occurs when multiple processes access shared data and the final result depends on the exact interleaving of execution.

In the spooler example, two processes can both read the same next-free-slot value and overwrite each other’s output file entry.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
A critical region is the part of a program where shared memory is accessed, and mutual exclusion requires no two processes enter simultaneously.
Operating Systems - Week 2 Lesson 1.pdf
Strict alternation avoids races but can violate progress because a process may be forced to wait even when the other is outside its critical region.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Peterson’s algorithm uses a turn variable and interested flags to ensure mutual exclusion without strict alternation for two processes.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Busy waiting wastes CPU time and can cause priority inversion when a high-priority process spins and prevents a low-priority lock holder from running.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Sleep and wakeup block a process until another wakes it, but naïve use in producer-consumer can still create race conditions.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Test-and-set style hardware instructions (such as XCHG) can implement spin locks by atomically checking and setting a lock variable.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Semaphores are integers whose down and up operations must be atomic to avoid races and correctly block or wake waiting processes.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
The down operation blocks when the semaphore is zero, and the up operation increments and wakes one sleeping process if any are waiting.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Binary semaphores are initialized to one and used to enforce mutual exclusion by down before entering and up after leaving the critical region.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
The bounded-buffer solution uses semaphores empty, full, and mutex to coordinate producer and consumer without lost wakeups.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
If semaphore downs are ordered incorrectly in producer-consumer, both processes can block forever, creating a deadlock.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
A mutex is a mutual exclusion lock with locked/unlocked states that guards a critical region by blocking threads that cannot acquire it.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Pthreads mutex calls include init, destroy, lock, trylock, and unlock, where unlock releases exactly one waiting thread.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Condition variables let threads sleep until a condition is met; pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the mutex while waiting.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Condition variables have no memory, so signaling when no thread is waiting loses the signal and can create subtle bugs.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Reader-writer synchronization can use a semaphore for database access and a reader count, but writers may starve if readers arrive continuously.
Operating Systems - Week 2 Lesson 2.pdf
A monitor is a higher-level synchronization construct that groups data and procedures and ensures only one process is active inside at a time.
Operating Systems - Week 2 Lesson 2.pdf
Message passing uses system calls send and receive; receivers may block until a message arrives or return an error immediately.
Chapter 2 - Andrew-S.-Tanenbaum-Modern-Operating-Systems.pdf
Distributed message passing must handle lost messages using acknowledgments and duplicates using sequence numbers.

Message systems also require unambiguous process naming and authentication to prevent communicating with imposters instead of real servers.

quiz.question: Which best defines a process in Tanenbaum’s model?
options: A passive program stored on disk
An executing program instance including PC, registers, and variables
A device driver running in kernel space
A shared memory buffer between applications
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A process is defined as an instance of an executing program with execution state such as PC and registers.

quiz.question: Why does multiprogramming create the illusion of parallelism on a single CPU?
options: Because the CPU runs multiple instructions simultaneously
Because the OS rapidly switches the CPU among processes
Because each process has its own physical core
Because interrupts prevent context switching
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Rapid context switching lets several processes make progress over time even though only one runs at an instant.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly contrasts a program and a process?
options: A program has state; a process is only code
A program is code; a process is the executing activity with state
A program always runs in kernel mode; a process always runs in user mode
A program is scheduled; a process is never scheduled
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A program is passive code, while a process is active execution with state and progress.

quiz.question: Which is NOT listed as a principal event that causes process creation?
options: System initialization
User request to create a new process
Initiation of a batch job
Cache miss in the CPU
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A cache miss is a hardware performance event, not a process creation event.

quiz.question: In UNIX, why is process creation typically a two-step fork() then execve()?
options: So the parent can always share writable memory with the child
So the child can adjust file descriptors for I/O redirection before execve()
So execve() can run in user mode without kernel involvement
So fork() can avoid creating a new process table entry
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Fork then execve lets the child manipulate file descriptors before replacing its program image.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a standard cause of process termination listed in Chapter 2?
options: Normal exit
Fatal error
Killed by another process
Disk fragmentation
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Disk fragmentation is not a termination cause; termination includes exit, errors, or being killed.

quiz.question: Which process state means the process cannot run until an external event occurs?
options: Running
Ready
Blocked
Initialized
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Blocked means the process is waiting for an event and cannot run even if the CPU is idle.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of the process table?
options: Store only file system directory entries
Store per-process state so processes can be stopped and restarted correctly
Store cache lines and replacement policy data
Store network routing tables for message passing
quiz.explanation: Correct because: The process table stores process state (PC, SP, registers, resources) needed for context switching.

quiz.question: Why are parts of interrupt handlers often written in assembly language?
options: Because assembly is required to render GUI graphics
Because saving registers and switching stacks is not reliably expressible in high-level code
Because semaphores only work in assembly
Because message passing requires assembly
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Low-level operations like saving CPU state and switching stacks are commonly handled in assembly.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes threads compared to processes?
options: Threads always have separate address spaces
Threads share the process address space but have their own stacks and execution state
Threads cannot block on I/O
Threads eliminate the need for synchronization
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Threads share address space and data but each thread has its own PC, registers, and stack.

quiz.question: When do threads provide the biggest performance benefit?
options: When all threads are purely CPU bound
When computation can overlap with I/O so one thread can run while another blocks
When the system has no scheduler
When all memory is read-only
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Threads help most when substantial computing and I/O overlap, allowing better utilization.

quiz.question: What is a race condition?
options: A deadlock where processes wait forever
A situation where results depend on exact interleaving of concurrent access to shared data
A guaranteed ordering of semaphore operations
A CPU scheduling algorithm for fairness
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Race conditions occur when timing/interleaving of shared-data access changes the final outcome.

quiz.question: In the spooler directory example, what is the core problem?
options: The printer daemon cannot read from disk
Two processes can compute the same next_free_slot and overwrite each other’s entry
The buffer is always empty so nothing prints
The OS prohibits shared memory entirely
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Both processes can read the same next slot, then one overwrites the other’s queued filename.

quiz.question: What is a critical region?
options: The section of code that must run in kernel mode
The part of a program where shared memory is accessed and must be protected
A file system directory used for spooling
A CPU cache line containing shared data
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A critical region is where shared data is accessed, requiring mutual exclusion to prevent races.

quiz.question: Why is strict alternation usually not considered a good general solution?
options: It can violate progress by forcing alternation even when one process is not interested
It requires a hypervisor
It eliminates mutual exclusion
It makes processes share writable memory
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Strict alternation can block a process even when the other is outside its critical region.

quiz.question: What is the main drawback of busy waiting solutions like spin locks?
options: They always cause deadlock immediately
They waste CPU time and can cause priority inversion
They require message passing to work
They only work on single-core systems
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Busy waiting consumes CPU and can prevent a lower-priority lock holder from running.

quiz.question: What do semaphores require to work correctly for synchronization?
options: Non-atomic up/down operations for flexibility
Atomic, indivisible up/down operations so state updates cannot interleave incorrectly
A GUI event loop
Per-thread private address spaces
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Semaphore operations must be atomic to prevent race conditions in synchronization.

quiz.question: What does down() do when the semaphore value is 0?
options: Increments the semaphore
Returns immediately with success
Blocks the calling process/thread until it can proceed
Deletes the semaphore
quiz.explanation: Correct because: When the semaphore is 0, down blocks until an up makes it possible to proceed.

quiz.question: What does up() do if processes are sleeping on that semaphore?
options: Wakes exactly one sleeping process and keeps the action atomic
Wakes all sleeping processes unconditionally
Blocks until the semaphore becomes negative
Resets the semaphore to 1 and exits
quiz.explanation: Correct because: up increments and wakes one sleeper if any are waiting, all as an indivisible action.

quiz.question: In the producer-consumer semaphore solution, what is mutex used for?
options: Counting empty slots in the buffer
Counting full slots in the buffer
Ensuring only one process accesses the buffer (critical region) at a time
Sending messages over the network
quiz.explanation: Correct because: mutex is the mutual exclusion semaphore guarding buffer access in the critical region.

quiz.question: What is a binary semaphore?
options: A semaphore initialized to 1 and used to enforce mutual exclusion
A semaphore that can only be used by two processes total
A semaphore implemented only in user space without kernel support
A semaphore that stores strings instead of integers
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A binary semaphore starts at 1 and is used to ensure only one process enters a critical region.

quiz.question: What happens if the producer reverses down(&empty) and down(&mutex) in the semaphore solution when the buffer is full?
options: Nothing changes because semaphore order never matters
The system guarantees it still works due to fairness scheduling
A deadlock can occur because the producer blocks holding mutex and the consumer then blocks on mutex too
It becomes a message-passing solution instead
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Reversing downs can make the producer block while holding mutex, preventing the consumer from accessing the buffer.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes a mutex?
options: A counting semaphore used to track buffer slots
A lock with locked/unlocked states that enforces mutual exclusion for a critical region
A network acknowledgment message
A scheduler policy to prevent starvation
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A mutex is a mutual exclusion lock used to guard critical sections from concurrent entry.

quiz.question: Which Pthreads call attempts to lock a mutex but returns an error instead of blocking if it is locked?
options: pthread_mutex_init
pthread_mutex_trylock
pthread_mutex_unlock
pthread_cond_wait
quiz.explanation: Correct because: pthread_mutex_trylock attempts to acquire the lock and fails immediately rather than blocking.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a condition variable?
options: Provide mutual exclusion by itself without any mutex
Allow threads to block until a condition becomes true, typically used with a mutex
Count resources like a semaphore does
Prevent context switches by disabling interrupts
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Condition variables enable waiting for conditions and are almost always used together with mutexes.

quiz.question: Why are condition variables said to have 'no memory'?
options: They cannot be stored in RAM
They do not preserve a signal if no thread is waiting at the time of the signal
They always wake all threads
They automatically log every wakeup event
quiz.explanation: Correct because: If a signal occurs when no thread is waiting, it is lost, so programmers must avoid missed signals.

quiz.question: What is a monitor?
options: A CPU instruction for atomic swap
A higher-level synchronization construct that ensures only one active process inside at a time
A file locking mode for shared libraries
A tool for compiling threaded programs
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Monitors group data and procedures with automatic mutual exclusion so only one execution is inside at once.

quiz.question: Which primitives define message passing in Chapter 2?
options: lock and unlock
sleep and wakeup
send and receive
fork and execve
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Message passing uses the system calls send(destination, &message) and receive(source, &message).

quiz.question: Why do message-passing systems often use acknowledgments and sequence numbers?
options: To enforce CPU scheduling fairness
To handle lost messages and detect duplicate retransmissions
To prevent cache misses
To guarantee mutual exclusion without locks
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Acknowledgments address loss, and sequence numbers let receivers distinguish duplicates from new messages.

quiz.question: In the readers-writers discussion, what risk is highlighted if readers continuously arrive?
options: Readers will starve forever
Writers may be delayed indefinitely (writer starvation)
The database becomes read-only permanently
Semaphores stop being atomic
quiz.explanation: Correct because: A steady stream of readers can prevent writers from acquiring exclusive access, causing writer starvation.

quiz.question: Which best connects processes/threads to hardware memory resources?
options: Threads always have separate address spaces so they cannot share memory
Processes require saving/restoring CPU and memory state so execution can resume after interrupts and scheduling
Memory access never affects concurrency correctness
Only message passing uses memory resources
quiz.explanation: Correct because: Process/thread execution relies on saving/restoring CPU state and managing memory/address-space state during switches.
